/.title: AI adoption by sector (Census BTOS)
/.company: U.S. employer businesses in the Census Bureau's Business Trends and Outlook Survey
/.problem: Can we predict what share of businesses in each sector will be using AI three and six months from now?
/.protocol_line: Every prediction is made from survey periods before its cutoff and scored on the periods three and six months after it; the design was frozen on the first quarter of the cutoffs.
/.situation: From September 2023 the Census Bureau asked businesses every two weeks whether they had used AI in producing goods or services in the last two weeks. Use rose in every sector, fastest in information, professional services and finance.
/.data_used: The Business Trends and Outlook Survey's biweekly estimates of the share of businesses that used AI, by two-digit NAICS sector, from September 2023 until the question's wording changed in November 2025 (public domain, U.S. Census Bureau).
/.intro: Rebuilds U.S. businesses as populations of firms, one population per sector. Each period a firm that does not use AI may start, and a firm that uses it may stop, with hazards that follow a diffusion curve: firms imitate adopters in their own sector and in the whole economy, and growth can slow as fewer non-users remain. From each cutoff the simulation carries every sector forward and is scored against the share of firms that actually reported AI use three and six months later. The alternative asks how much faster manufacturing and retail would adopt if an adoption programme doubled their firms' hazard of starting.
/.world: Fifteen sectors, each a population of 1,000 simulated firms that use AI or not; the national share of firms using AI is the economy-wide signal that firms in every sector imitate.
/.source: manifests/sources.json (U.S. Census Bureau, Business Trends and Outlook Survey, AI Core Questions; public domain)

evaluation.cutoffs: 14 cutoffs, one every four weeks, from 2024-06-17 to 2025-06-16 (survey collection start)
evaluation.horizons: 6 and 13 biweekly periods (about 3 and 6 months) after the last observed period
evaluation.calibration: at each cutoff, backtests whose targets fall before it

scenarios.title: AI adoption as it happened: every sector carried forward from the cutoff
scenarios.description: From each cutoff, carry each sector's firms forward for six months: non-users start using AI and users stop with the hazards of the diffusion path calibrated on the periods before the cutoff. Nothing after the cutoff is known to the simulation.

scenarios.title: What if an adoption programme had doubled manufacturing and retail firms' hazard of starting to use AI?
scenarios.short_title: Adoption programme in manufacturing and retail
scenarios.summary: Non-using firms in manufacturing and retail trade start using AI at twice the simulated hazard from the cutoff; same cutoffs and seeds.
scenarios.description: A programme (training, subsidised tools) doubles the probability that a non-using manufacturing or retail firm starts using AI in each period. Every other sector, and the firms that already use AI, behave as in the simulation of what happened. The size of the effect is authored, not estimated.

takeaways: On 10 held-out cutoffs (255 predictions) the simulation's error was 1.37 pp, lower than the best standard method (bass diffusion, 1.52 pp): 9.9% less error.
Accuracy, 100 x (1 - error / mean actual): 85.2% for the simulation and 83.6% for bass diffusion.
Over all 14 cutoffs, including the 4 used to design it: 1.25 pp against 1.40 pp (bass diffusion).
3 months ahead (6 periods): 1.11 pp for the simulation, 1.19 pp for bass diffusion; 82% of actual outcomes inside the simulation's 90% range.
6 months ahead (13 periods): 1.74 pp for the simulation, 1.98 pp for bass diffusion; 73% of actual outcomes inside the simulation's 90% range.

/scenarios.title: AI adoption as it happened: every sector carried forward from the cutoff
/scenarios.description: From each cutoff, carry each sector's firms forward for six months: non-users start using AI and users stop with the hazards of the diffusion path calibrated on the periods before the cutoff. Nothing after the cutoff is known to the simulation.

/scenarios.title: What if an adoption programme had doubled manufacturing and retail firms' hazard of starting to use AI?
/scenarios.short_title: Adoption programme in manufacturing and retail
/scenarios.summary: Non-using firms in manufacturing and retail trade start using AI at twice the simulated hazard from the cutoff; same cutoffs and seeds.
/scenarios.description: A programme (training, subsidised tools) doubles the probability that a non-using manufacturing or retail firm starts using AI in each period. Every other sector, and the firms that already use AI, behave as in the simulation of what happened. The size of the effect is authored, not estimated.

properties.description: The company or group being simulated. Root of the org-unit tree.
A division, department or team. Units nest (part_of) and hold people and roles.
An employee, played as a digital twin: real covariates, a fixed trait layer, weekly latent states and a seat whose policy makes its decisions. Archetypes when the data has no individuals.
A job in this organisation (e.g. purchasing clerk, software engineer). Bound to one O*NET-SOC occupation; performs the instance's activities.
An O*NET-SOC 31.0 occupation, the shared vocabulary that lets roles in different companies be compared.
O*NET generalized work activity: the top level of the activity hierarchy (41 items).
O*NET intermediate work activity (332 items), between GWAs and DWAs.
O*NET detailed work activity (2,087 items). Every instance activity maps to at least one DWA.
An O*NET occupation-specific task statement.
Something a role does in this organisation on the simulated clock (an event-log step, a customer call, a code review). Carries a weight and a remote-feasibility flag.
The unit of work that flows through activities: a purchase-order line, a case, a ticket.
A document or output an activity produces (invoice, merged code change, review).
A tool or software system (ERP, CRM, code repository) that exposes capabilities.
One thing a system can do, in the MCP sense; activities use capabilities. Automating a capability is a policy lever.
A place work happens: an office, a home, a plant. Hybrid-work policies move people between locations.
A vendor, client or customer outside the organisation that interacts with its activities.
A communication between people (email, chat, meeting invitation).
An intervention or scenario lever: a work-from-home offer, an automation, a hiring wave. Affects roles, activities, capabilities, units or locations.
One recorded occurrence on the clock: a person performed an activity on a work item at a time. The trace is a sequence of events.
A latent, time-varying quantity attached to a person: job satisfaction, work-life balance, attachment, commute burden. Updated weekly by the kernel.
